metadata.title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision

problem.value: Unsupervised pre-trained audio encoders lack equivalent performant decoders, which makes a fine-tuning stage necessary to perform tasks like speech recognition.

evidence.quote: These pre-trained audio encoders learn high-quality representations of speech, but because they are purely unsupervised they lack an equivalently performant decoder mapping those representations to usable outputs, necessitating a finetuning stage in order to actually perform a task such as speech recognition 1 .

contributions.value: Scaling weakly supervised speech recognition to 680,000 hours of labeled audio data.

evidence.quote: In this work we close that gap, scaling weakly supervised speech recognition the next order of magnitude to 680,000 hours of labeled audio data.

contributions.value: Broadening the scope of weakly supervised pre-training to be multilingual and multitask.

evidence.quote: In addition to scale, our work also focuses on broadening the scope of weakly supervised pre-training beyond English-only speech recognition to be both multilingual and multitask.

contributions.value: Releasing inference code and models to serve as a foundation for further research.

evidence.quote: To serve as a foundation for further research on robust speech recognition, we release inference code and models at the following URL: https://github.com/openai/ whisper.

method_summary.value: An off-the-shelf encoder-decoder Transformer architecture is used as the core model to avoid confounding findings with model design changes.

evidence.quote: We chose an encoder-decoder Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as this architecture has been well validated to scale reliably.

method_summary.value: Input audio is processed as an 80-channel log-magnitude Mel spectrogram computed on 25-millisecond windows with a 10-millisecond stride.

evidence.quote: All audio is re-sampled to 16,000 Hz, and an 80-channel logmagnitude Mel spectrogram representation is computed on 25-millisecond windows with a stride of 10 milliseconds.

method_summary.value: A minimalist data pre-processing and training approach is used to predict raw transcripts without standardization, removing the need for inverse text normalization.

evidence.quote: In contrast to a lot of work on speech recognition, we train Whisper models to predict the raw text of transcripts without any significant standardization, relying on the expressiveness of sequence-to-sequence models to learn to map between utterances and their transcribed form.

method_summary.value: A multitask sequence-to-sequence format uses special tokens fed into the decoder to specify tasks like transcription, translation, language identification, and timestamps.

evidence.quote: We use a simple format to specify all tasks and conditioning information as a sequence of input tokens to the decoder.

method_summary.value: Models are optimized using AdamW, gradient norm clipping, and linear learning rate decay with data parallelism and FP16 precision.

evidence.quote: Models were trained with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) and gradient norm clipping (Pascanu et al., 2013) with a linear learning rate decay to zero after a warmup over the first 2048 updates.

novelty.value: The approach uses a minimalist data pre-processing pipeline that trains on raw transcripts without significant standardization or inverse text normalization.

evidence.quote: In contrast to a lot of work on speech recognition, we train Whisper models to predict the raw text of transcripts without any significant standardization, relying on the expressiveness of sequence-to-sequence models to learn to map between utterances and their transcribed form.

novelty.value: A single multitask model replaces many individual stages of a traditional speech processing pipeline by handling transcription, translation, voice activity detection, and language identification.

evidence.quote: The multitask training format uses a set of special tokens that serve as task specifiers or classification targets, as further explained in Section 2.3.

To study the performance of Whisper more broadly we also report performance on the Fleurs dataset (Conneau et al., 2022).
We study the translation capabilities of Whisper models by measuring their performance on the X→en subset of CoVoST2 (Wang et al., 2020b).

On VoxPopuli, however, Whisper significantly underperforms prior work and only beats the VP-10K+FT baseline from the original paper.
We compare with Maestro, mSLAM, and XLS-R, the highest-performing prior work.
Speech recognition research typically evaluates and compares systems based on the word error rate (WER) metric.
We achieve a new state of the art of 29.1 BLEU zero-shot without using any of the CoVoST2 training data.

limitations.value: Speech recognition performance is poor for many languages due to a lack of training data.

evidence.quote: As Figure 3 shows, Whisper's speech recognition performance is still quite poor on many languages.

future_work.value: Fine-tuning models on supervised datasets or using reinforcement learning to optimize decoding performance.

evidence.quote: Although the decoding details discussed in Section 4.5 help significantly, we suspect fine-tuning Whisper models on a high-quality supervised dataset and/or using reinforcement learning to more directly optimize for decoding performance could help further reduce these errors.

future_work.value: Targeted efforts to increase the amount of training data for lower-resource languages.

evidence.quote: A targeted effort at increasing the amount of data for these rarer languages could result in a large improvement to average speech recognition performance even with only a small increase in our overall training dataset size.

future_work.value: Studying fine-tuning to potentially improve results where high-quality supervised speech data exists.

evidence.quote: While this is a crucial setting to study due to it being representative of general reliability, for many domains where high-quality supervised speech data does exist, it is likely that results can be improved further by fine-tuning.

future_work.value: Investigating whether benefits stem from the encoder, decoder, or both through targeted ablations.

evidence.quote: This could be studied by either ablating various design components of Whisper, such as training a decoder-less CTC model, or by studying how the performance of existing speech recognition encoders such as wav2vec 2.0 change when used together with a language model.
To serve as a foundation for further research on robust speech recognition, we release inference code and models at the following URL: https://github.com/openai/ whisper.

claims.value: The models generalize well to standard benchmarks and are competitive with prior fully supervised results in a zero-shot setting.

evidence.quote: When scaled to 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask supervision, the resulting models generalize well to standard benchmarks and are often competitive with prior fully supervised results but in a zeroshot transfer setting without the need for any finetuning.

claims.value: A computer vision model showed a 9.2% increase in object classification accuracy when fine-tuned on ImageNet without improvement on seven other natural image datasets.

evidence.quote: In a particularly disturbing example, Radford et al. ( 2021) documented a 9.2% increase in object classification accuracy when fine-tuning a computer vision model on the ImageNet dataset (Russakovsky et al., 2015) without observing any improvement in average accuracy when classifying the same objects on seven other natural image datasets.

claims.value: SpeechStew mixes 7 pre-existing datasets totaling 5,140 hours of supervision.

evidence.quote: SpeechStew (Chan et al., 2021) mixes together 7 pre-existing datasets totalling 5,140 hours of supervision.
